title: Solvents, stains, finishes and fire risk in timber restoration
audience: Timber floor restoration workers who handle stains, sealers, strippers and solvents, and the supervisors who approve them.
learningOutcomes: Read a product label and safety data sheet before use, and state the controls they require.
Identify the ignition sources that must be removed from a timber sanding or finishing area.
Describe safe storage and disposal of flammable products and contaminated rags.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Queensland, Chemical reaction exposes worker to toxic gas (no date on page; incident dated March 2022); SafeWork NSW, Wood dust: health hazards and control (wood safety kit) (published 20 September 2018; last modified 11 July 2023); NSW Government, LeadSmart: renovating and maintenance (published 18 May 2026; last modified 20 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Read the label and the safety data sheet first
instruction.body: Timber restoration uses stains, oils, sealers, strippers, solvents and cleaners, and each has its own hazards. Before opening a product, read its label and its safety data sheet (SDS) for ventilation, personal protective equipment, storage, incompatibilities and disposal. WorkSafe Queensland's incident alert (no date shown on the page; incident dated March 2022) advises checking the label and SDS for how to handle, store and respond in an emergency, and says SDS should be kept within easy reach of workers. Do not mix products or change their strength to get a different result. Use only products the SDS and the manufacturer approve for the floor and the finish.

instruction.heading: Vapours in enclosed rooms
instruction.body: Solvent and stain vapours build up in closed rooms. The ventilation the job needs is set by the SDS and the job plan. Do not work in a closed room with a product that needs ventilation until the plan has been confirmed.

instruction.heading: Ignition sources and dust
instruction.body: Open flames, sparks and hot surfaces can ignite vapours. SafeWork NSW (last modified 11 July 2023) warns that wood dust can create an explosion risk, and advises keeping flames and sparks away from areas where dust is produced. Remove open flames, spark-producing tools and unnecessary heaters from the work area unless the plan approves them.

instruction.heading: No open-flame stripping
instruction.body: Do not use an open-flame torch to strip an old finish. NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) says open-flame torches create lead fumes, and advises the lowest setting and no lingering in one spot for a heat gun. If a heat tool is approved in the plan, follow that advice.

instruction.heading: Storage and disposal
instruction.body: Store flammable products according to the approved storage procedure and the relevant standard. Used rags and cloths that have been in contact with oil or finish must be placed in a labelled container and disposed of as the approved waste procedure says.

procedure: Read the label and SDS before opening any product, and confirm the ventilation and PPE it requires.
Remove open flames, sparks, unnecessary heaters and other ignition sources from the work area.
Keep only the products needed in the room, and store the rest according to the approved storage procedure.
Ventilate as the SDS and the plan require, and confirm the ventilation equipment is not itself an ignition source.
Place used rags and waste in a labelled container and dispose of them according to the approved waste procedure, not in an enclosed space.
Record the product name, batch, SDS checked, ventilation used and ignition sources removed.

workedExamples.situation: A worker wants to use a solvent-based stripper in a bedroom with the window closed, and a heater is switched on near the door. The job is due to finish today.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must happen before the stripper is opened?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. The closed room needs ventilation that the SDS and the plan require, and the heater is an ignition source near the vapour. Turn the heater off and move it away, confirm a ventilation method approved in the plan, and check the SDS for PPE. If the plan cannot provide the ventilation, the job waits. Do not hurry to finish because of the deadline.

equipmentAndPpe: Product labels and SDS for each product in use
Ventilation equipment as set by the plan
Fire extinguisher suitable for the area, as set by the plan.
Labelled, lidded waste container for rags and residue

commonErrors.error: Using an open-flame torch to strip an old finish.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not use an open flame. Use the non-flame method approved in the assessment.

commonErrors.error: Leaving oily rags in a pile in the room.
commonErrors.prevention: Place them in a labelled container and dispose of them per the approved waste procedure.

commonErrors.error: Mixing two products to get a different colour or strength.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only products the SDS and manufacturer approve, and do not mix them.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) says open-flame torches create lead fumes, and advises a low setting and no lingering on one spot for a heat gun.

SafeWork NSW (last modified 11 July 2023) warns that wood dust can create an explosion risk, and advises keeping flames and sparks away from dust-generating areas. An earlier industry-body guide is not an official source and is not relied on.

qualityStandard: The SDS is read and recorded for every product before it is opened.
Ignition sources are removed from the work area, and the removal is recorded.
Waste and rags are disposed of according to the approved procedure.
documentationEvidence: Product and SDS register for the job
Ventilation and ignition source check record
Waste disposal record for rags and residue
summary: Read the label and SDS before opening any product.
Remove ignition sources. Do not use an open-flame torch.
Store and dispose of flammable products and rags as the approved procedure says.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: WorkSafe Queensland, Chemical reaction exposes worker to toxic gas (no date on page; incident dated March 2022); SafeWork NSW, Wood dust: health hazards and control (wood safety kit) (published 20 September 2018; last modified 11 July 2023); NSW Government, LeadSmart: renovating and maintenance (published 18 May 2026; last modified 20 July 2026).

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the first check before opening a stain or solvent?
options: Open it and smell it
Ask the client
Read the label and the SDS
Pour a sample on the floor

knowledgeChecks.question: Why avoid open flames when stripping old finishes?
options: They dry the finish out far too fast on the job
They make the wood brittle and cracked on the job
They are cheaper to run than the other tools
They can create hazardous fumes or ignite vapours

knowledgeChecks.question: What does SafeWork NSW advise to reduce the risk of a dust explosion?
options: Keep flames and sparks away from areas where dust is generated
It cannot burn at any temperature in the workshop or the house
It is always safe to leave in a room with the door open
It only burns in summer weather conditions and in the heat of the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Which storage rule is correct for flammable products?
options: Keep any container on the bench for easy use during the job today
Store them per the approved storage procedure and the relevant standard
Keep them in the vehicle with the windows up and the doors shut
Pour leftovers down the drain at the end of the job each day

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker mixes two products to get a darker colour. What is correct?
options: Mix them if they look similar in colour and smell on the job
Mix them because the client asked for a darker shade on the day of the job
Use only products the SDS and manufacturer approve, and do not mix them
Mix them in a closed room with the door shut and the window closed
